rules.statement: In a test project, don't report a stub, fake, fixture or sample type that only one test file needs for being nested in that file's test class: the test conventions make it a `private sealed` nested type there, and the no-nested-types rule covers production code only.
rules.why: The test rules ask for single-file stubs, fakes and samples to be private sealed nested types, so moving them out would break the convention.
rules.check: Before reporting a nested type in a test class, check whether it is private sealed and used by only that test file. If it is, don't report it.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't report the null-forgiving operator where a test passes `null` to a non-nullable parameter or receiver to prove it throws `ArgumentNullException`, because the build bans `!` outside test projects only. Elsewhere in tests, narrow nullable values with `?? throw new InvalidOperationException(...)` naming what is missing, or with `Assert.NotNull`, instead of `!`.
rules.why: Proving a null guard needs `!` to get past nullable analysis. Elsewhere, a missing value should fail with a clear message, not an unclear NullReferenceException.
rules.check: For `!` in test code, check whether it exists to pass null on purpose to a null-guarded API. If so, don't report it. Report `!` on lookup results such as `GetString()!` or `GetProperty(...)!`.

rules.statement: Dispose a local disposable that a method owns, such as an `HttpClient` created in a test, with a `using var` declaration, but don't ask for `using` on a disposable that a helper creates and returns to its caller.
rules.why: An owned disposable should be released when it goes out of scope, but a helper that hands its client to the caller doesn't own it and must not dispose it.
rules.check: Look for `var x = Create...()` locals of IDisposable types that are never disposed. Before reporting, check whether the method returns the value.

rules.statement: Don't put the `$` prefix on a string literal that has no interpolation holes.
rules.why: It suggests a value was meant to be interpolated, which misleads readers.
rules.check: Look for `$"..."` strings that contain no `{...}` placeholders.

rules.statement: Derive byte offsets and slice lengths into a binary format from the format's named size constants, or from a named constant whose comment explains how it follows from them, instead of hard-coded numeric literals, in tests as well as in production code.
rules.why: If the format changes, a literal offset can drift from it. A test could then compare the wrong bytes and still pass.
rules.check: Look for slices or offsets such as `[..15]` or `KeyIdSizeBytes + 60` whose numbers stand for sizes of format fields.

rules.statement: Put an explanatory comment in the method whose behaviour it describes, not in a neighbouring helper that does something else.
rules.why: A misplaced comment misleads readers about which code does what.
rules.check: Check that each comment's claims match the code it sits in, for example a comment about creating rows inside a method that creates no rows.

rules.statement: Don't report whitespace-only re-padding of a Markdown table when an added or changed row is wider than the table's column, because tables are kept aligned.
rules.why: An aligned table has to be re-padded when a new cell is wider than its column, so the whitespace change is needed.
rules.check: Before reporting table re-padding in a Markdown diff, check whether any new row is wider than the old column width. Report it only when no row needs the extra width.

rules.statement: Don't report a private method with a single call site for taking more than three data parameters, or for being one sequential body. The few-parameters rule exempts such helpers from needing a parameter object, and steps that share local state in a fixed order can stay in one method.
rules.why: The production conventions say a private single-call-site helper isn't worth a parameter object. Splitting a sequence whose steps share state would only pass that state across more boundaries.
rules.check: Before reporting parameter count or a long body, check whether the method is private and has one call site, and whether its steps share locals such as a buffer, a store manager or a token.

rules.statement: Don't report a private builder method for taking more than three parameters when those parameters are the fields of the object it builds, and splitting it into per-kind factories would repeat a large initializer.
rules.why: The arguments are the constructed object's own data, so grouping or splitting them only adds duplication.
rules.check: Check whether the parameters map directly to members of the object being constructed, and whether splitting the builder would copy the initializer for each caller.

rules.statement: Don't report pure helpers in an Abstractions or contracts package when they belong to its value types or contracts, such as a `TryParse` that inverts the type's `ToString`, or an extension method composed only from the contract's members, with no dependencies or state.
rules.why: These helpers are part of the value type or contract itself, so they don't blur the contracts-only boundary.
rules.check: Before reporting behaviour in an Abstractions package, check whether it needs any dependency or state beyond the package's own types. Report it only if it does.

rules.statement: Don't report a `*Manager` type name as a catch-all when the type owns one well-defined concept, such as the lifecycle of one kind of entity or a unit-of-work seam.
rules.why: The naming rule targets catch-all types. A manager with one cohesive responsibility follows established naming such as `IStoreManager`.
rules.check: Before reporting a Manager suffix, list the type's members and check whether they all serve a single concept.
